analysis.one_liner: Pays colleges to switch to the cheaper federal student loan program and use the savings for student grants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction with 34 cosponsors from both parties, it was referred to a House subcommittee in June 2007 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, two federal programs issued student loans: one where the government lent directly to students, and one where private banks issued loans backed by federal guarantees and subsidies. The guaranteed-bank program cost taxpayers more per loan. This bill would have paid colleges a reward worth at least half of the federal savings for moving their students into the cheaper loan program, required them to stay there for five years, and directed the reward money into extra Pell Grants and need-based grants for lower- and middle-income graduate students. The bill included a trigger requiring that total payments not exceed the actual federal savings, so it could not add to the deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: Students: Pell Grant recipients would get supplemental grants, and lower- and middle-income graduate students could receive need-based grants. Taxpayers would benefit from switching loans to the cheaper federal program. Colleges would receive reward payments worth at least 50% of the federal savings they generated.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Education to run a Student Aid Reward Program paying colleges to participate in whichever federal loan program is most cost-effective for taxpayers.
Each participating college would receive a payment worth at least 50% of the savings the federal government gains from the cheaper loan program instead of the more expensive one.

Colleges receiving payments would be required, where appropriate, to pass the money to students as supplements to Pell Grants, and could also use it for need-based grants to lower- and middle-income graduate students.
The bill includes a cost-neutrality trigger: total reward payments could not exceed the federal savings generated by the program, so payments were funded entirely by the efficiencies created.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders in the guaranteed-loan program would lose federal loan volume and the associated subsidy stream as colleges moved borrowers to the cheaper direct program. Colleges that preferred to stay in the guaranteed program would forgo the reward payments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Guaranteed student loan lenders and banks

drawbacks.text: The grant aid is indirect and conditional: colleges, not students, receive the reward payments first, and the requirement that they 'where appropriate' pass funds to Pell recipients gives institutions discretion over whether and how much reaches students.
Colleges taking payments must commit to the cheaper loan program for five years, which some institutions viewed as limiting their flexibility to choose loan programs on behalf of their students.

Payments are based on the Secretary's estimates of federal savings, with later adjustments that could reduce future payments if actual savings fell short, creating uncertainty for colleges budgeting around the rewards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was designed to be self-funding: it converts federal savings from cheaper loan delivery into student grants, with a trigger preventing payments from exceeding those savings. The main weakness is that aid flows through colleges first and depends on their choices and on accurate estimates of savings. Still, the core trade is straightforward — federal money now spent subsidizing a more expensive loan channel would be redirected to grants for needy students.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2007, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Higher Education subcommittee in June 2007, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) and Rep. Thomas Petri (R-WI) introduced the bill on February 13, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On June 5, 2007, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education, Lifelong Learning, and Competitiveness, where it remained without further action.
The bill attracted 34 cosponsors, 31 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but no vote was ever held on it in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private lenders in the federally guaranteed student loan program kept their federal-subsidized loan volume, and taxpayers and students never received the savings or the extra grants the bill would have redirected.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-7) and bill sponsor, chair of the House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through referral.

for.name: Rep. Thomas Petri
for.what_they_did: Joined Miller in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Education and Labor Subcommittee on Higher Education, Lifelong Learning, and Competitiveness
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 5, 2007 and took no further action; the bill was never reported out for a floor vote.

against.name: Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) industry — banks, loan servicers, and guarantee agencies
against.role: Lenders in the federally guaranteed student loan program
against.what_they_did: Lobbied through the era to preserve the guaranteed-loan program and its federal subsidies, which the bill would have drained as colleges switched to direct lending.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape can only be read from cosponsorship: 31 of the 34 cosponsors were Democrats, though the bill was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican together.

industries.industry: Guaranteed student loan lenders (banks and FFEL guarantee agencies)
industries.note: Every college that switched to the cheaper direct loan program under the bill would move loan volume away from bank-issued, federally guaranteed loans, cutting lenders' subsidized business. The federal subsidies in that channel cost taxpayers more per loan than direct lending, so the industry's interest ran against the bill's savings and student grants.

Institutions would receive reward payments worth at least 50% of the federal savings they generated, and could pass those funds to students as grant supplements. In exchange they had to commit to the cheaper loan program for five years.
